newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-WOODS HOPES HE HAS THE CLOUT TO TAME CONGRESSIONAL.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-WOODS HOPES HE HAS THE CLOUT TO TAME CONGRESSIONAL.

text.p: You always needed plenty of clout to play at Congressional.
And that's what Tiger Woods is banking on as he gears up for a run at the second leg of golf's elusive Grand Slam at the U.S. Open starting on Thursday.

Woods, the 21-year-old runaway winner of the Masters, is golf's biggest hitter and he ought to feel right at home at Congressional, the longest ever U.S. Open course at 7,213 yards despite having only two par-5s on a par-70 card.
Power has always figured in Congressional's persona.

The founding life members of the exclusive club included U.S. presidents Warren Harding, Woodrow Wilson, William Howard Taft and Calvin Coolidge. John D. Rockefeller and Alfred duPont surely helped cover the club's bottom line.

Recent presidents have also tried their games on the sweeping hills of these 343 acres just outside Washington -- Bill Clinton, George Bush, Gerald Ford, Richard Nixon, Lyndon Johnson, John Kennedy and Dwight Eisenhower, for example.

This week, 156 of the world's best players will ply their skills on the course, which is armed by U.S. Golf Association strategists with the single greatest defence against the long ball in golf -- deep, thick, ball-swallowing rough.
Woods drew thousands of spectators along his solo tour of the front nine in practice on Monday.

Egged on by roaring fans to shoot for the green with his second shot at the 607-yard par-5 ninth hole, the young, black superstar surveyed the 281 yards he had to the flag, teed the ball up and hit driver again, finishing pin-high though off- track with his mammoth approach shot.

Control, of course, is what wins U.S. Opens and it remains to be seen if Woods can harnass all that power and play the sort of measured game that makes Nick Faldo, Colin Montgomerie and patient big-hitters like Tom Lehman and Davis Love perennial contenders.

At the Masters, Woods drove the ball erratically at times but was always able to recover on a forgiving Augusta National layout that is bereft of rough and allows for creative escapes from errant tee balls. Woods waltzed to a 12-shot triumph.
The challengers who hope to knock Woods off the Grand Slam trail this week agree that Congressional, and the nasty U.S. Open rough, will pose a more formidable test.
"The rough is as long as any I've seen at any U.S. Open," said lefty contender Phil Mickelson. "The rough is like hay out there."
New Zealander Frank Nobilo said: "The rough is very thick, very lush. It's probably the worst I've seen.
"There is a huge reward for straight drives. You're going to have to be very straight."
Former PGA champion Steve Elkington of Australia said dealing with the rough takes its toll on the players.
"It's as much a physical test as a mental test," said Elkington, who won The Players Championship this year and stands second to Woods on the U.S. tour's money list.
"It's hard to look out there and know that if you get in it it's basically a stroke lost."
Nobilo said the greens, shaved down to increase speed, added to the daunting challenge of playing successfully out of the rough.
"Many of the greens have spines running through the middle," Nobilo noted. "You've got to be able to fly it to the right sections. It's brutal."
Defending champion Steve Jones, who came through in a last hole duel with Lehman last year at Oakland Hills, offered this rough advice for Woods and the rest of the Congressional combatants.
"Don't get in it. Definitely don't get in it."
